items.prompt: What is management of managers?
choices: Leading a team of managers so each runs their own team better
Managing a very large group of individual engineers directly, with no managers in between
Doing the work of several managers yourself to save time
items.explanation: Your team is made of managers, and the job is to make each one more effective, not to run their teams.

items.prompt: After her promotion, how many managers report to Renata?
choices: Eight
Three
Twenty-four
items.explanation: Three managers report to her. They run twenty-four engineers between them.

items.prompt: Whom does Renata manage directly after the promotion?
choices: All twenty-four engineers
The one engineer she helped
The three managers
items.explanation: Her direct reports are the three managers; the engineers report to them.

items.prompt: What is second-order leadership?
choices: Your decisions reach engineers only after a manager has interpreted them
Leading a project from a second office or time zone, as a backup lead
Taking over the second half of a stalled project
items.explanation: A decision lands on a manager first, who adapts it before anything reaches an engineer.

items.prompt: What does reaching past a manager mean?
choices: Asking your own manager for extra budget or headcount for a new project
Directing someone on another manager's team without involving that manager
Promoting one manager above the rest of their peers
items.explanation: It means going straight to a manager's report and leaving the manager out of the loop.

items.prompt: Why was Renata's Slack rescue the wrong move?
choices: Unblocking people quickly is never part of good management
Slack is not a suitable place to discuss any work
It bypassed the engineer's manager and signaled distrust
items.explanation: The speed was fine; the layer was wrong, and the manager read it as distrust.

items.prompt: How did the engineer's manager learn about the rescue?
choices: From the engineer
From Renata's weekly summary email
From a post in the team channel
items.explanation: The manager heard it from the engineer, which made the bypass sting more.

items.prompt: Does good intent make reaching past a manager harmless?
choices: Yes, as long as the engineer is grateful afterward
No, it still erodes the manager's standing
Yes, provided it only ever happens one time
items.explanation: The effect on the manager does not depend on the intent behind the shortcut.

items.prompt: Renata's new report Sam manages six engineers. A stuck engineer on Sam's team messages Renata directly because she is fast. What is the best response?
choices: Help briefly if it is urgent, loop Sam in at once, and agree how such requests should route
Fix it quietly and tell nobody, so Sam is not embarrassed by the stuck engineer
Refuse to answer anyone outside her direct reports, however urgent the block is
Fix it, then ask Sam to remind his team that Renata is the fastest option
items.explanation: She can respond to a real block, but looping Sam in keeps his role visible. Silence or a refusal each damage something different.
items.reference:
Before and after the promotion
8 engineers reported to Renata, now 3 managers do
24 engineers reached, but only through those 3
dotted line = reaching past a manager
Why: her lever is now each manager's capability, and every direct shortcut weakens the manager she depends on.
items.learnMore:
The layer is the job

A manager of managers produces results through other people's decisions. Speed at fixing things stops being the measure; how capable each manager has become takes its place.

Common mistake

Treating the new role as the old one with more people. The same habit one layer up reads as distrust.
items.reflection: Think of a time someone above you skipped past your manager (or you skipped past someone). What did it do to trust on both sides?

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the Slack rescue damaged the relationship, even though the ticket got fixed?
choices: It broke a rule that directors may never read engineers' threads, whatever the reason
It told the manager their judgment about their own team is optional
It proved Renata no longer understands the technical work her teams do
It took credit for the fix away from the engineer involved in the block
items.explanation: The fix was not the issue; the message about whose team it is was. Directors reading threads is not itself the problem.

choices: Directors cannot legitimately have any visibility into the individual work of engineers
Weekly status is too frequent and should be monthly at her level
Her outcomes come from managers, so she should track how effective they are
Managers cannot be trusted to report accurately on the real progress of their own teams
items.explanation: Visibility still matters, but the lever has moved to the managers. Tracking each engineer weekly rebuilds the old job.

choices: Engineers lose access to anyone with real authority
Y's calendar will be too empty to be productive
Y's engineers will refuse to talk to their own managers
Managers stop owning decisions and wait for Y to act
items.explanation: When shortcuts are the norm, managers learn their decisions will be overridden, so they stop making them.

items.prompt: Which is the coaching move for a report who is missing expectations?
choices: Ask the manager what they have said so far, then plan the next talk together
Meet the report yourself, restate the expectations, and follow up with them directly
Move the report to a different team
items.explanation: Coaching keeps the manager as the one holding the conversation, with Renata helping them prepare.

items.prompt: What does fixing directly produce when it becomes the default?
choices: A manager who grows steadily more confident and needs her less over time
A manager who escalates because escalating gets it handled
A team that no longer has any problems at all
items.explanation: Repeated rescues teach the manager that handing the problem up works.

items.prompt: Why can't Renata just fix every team's problem?
choices: Fixing problems is forbidden for every director in the company, in all cases
Managers flatly refuse to ever ask her for help
She cannot scale, and fixes teach the managers nothing
items.explanation: Her time is finite; the lasting lever is the managers' capability.

items.prompt: A manager says 'just tell me what to do.' What is the coaching response?
choices: Work the problem through, asking what they would try
Give a complete, step-by-step answer so the manager can act on it at once
Tell them to work it out alone
items.explanation: Handing over the answer repeats the rescue habit; working it through builds the skill.

items.prompt: Is stepping in directly ever right?
choices: No, never, whatever the situation turns out to be and however severe it gets
Yes, in a true emergency the manager cannot handle
Yes, whenever doing it herself would be faster
items.explanation: A real emergency is the narrow exception, not speed alone.

items.prompt: What should Renata do after stepping in during an emergency?
choices: Say nothing so the manager feels no pressure
Take over that team's decisions for good, since the manager seems unready
Tell the manager and go back over it with them
items.explanation: Telling and debriefing keeps the manager informed and learning.

items.prompt: What is abdication in this unit's sense?
choices: Leaving a manager to sink alone and calling it coaching
Handing a team over to a newly hired manager
Promoting a strong manager very quickly
items.explanation: Coaching still means knowing what is happening; abdication drops that.

items.prompt: A manager's 1:1s have become status updates. Which is a coaching question?
choices: Why do you run such poor and unhelpful 1:1s?
What are you hoping to get out of your 1:1s?
Can I sit in and run the next one for you?
items.explanation: A question about the manager's own goal lets them find the gap themselves.

items.prompt: Team B's manager, Lena, has run two sprint plans that overcommit the team. Renata thinks she knows the cause. Which action best builds Lena's skill?
choices: Ask Lena to walk through how she planned, and let her find the overcommit
Redo the plan herself and share the corrected version with Lena afterward
Tell Lena the cause in one sentence and move on to the next topic on the list
Attend the next planning session and run it herself while Lena watches and takes notes
items.explanation: A walkthrough keeps Lena as the planner and surfaces the cause. The other options hand over or demonstrate the answer.
items.reference:
Fix or coach?
fix directly = fast now, manager learns nothing
coach = slower now, manager is stronger next time
true emergency = act, but tell the manager and debrief
Why: the lever is the manager's capability, so the default is to work through them, with a narrow openly-stated exception.
items.learnMore:
Coaching has an exception, not a loophole

A real emergency can justify acting directly. What keeps it honest is telling the manager and going back over it, so the manager is not simply replaced.

Common mistake

Treating every problem as a coaching moment, or calling neglect coaching. Both leave a manager unsupported.
items.reflection: When did someone hand you the answer instead of working it through with you? What did you learn from it, and what did you not?

items.prompt: A manager has a safety-related incident on their team and is unsure how to respond. What fits this unit's guidance best?
choices: Coach them through it by asking questions over the next two weeks, as usual
Step in directly, say so openly, and debrief the manager afterward
Stay out of it so the manager's authority is not undermined
Step in quietly and let the manager believe they handled it
items.explanation: A real emergency is the exception. Openness and a debrief keep the manager from being replaced silently.

choices: Conclude that coaching never works and take over all of the team's recurring problems
Stop checking in entirely so the manager has the space to work it out alone
Offer closer support, such as observing a conversation, while the manager still leads
Share the problem with the manager's whole team to apply some pressure
items.explanation: Closer support is the right escalation. Taking over replaces the manager; withdrawing is abdication.

choices: Renata asks a manager three questions before offering an opinion
Renata asks to see the plan before the manager acts on it
Renata steps in during a real emergency and then debriefs
Renata says 'figure it out' and does not look at the team again for a quarter
items.explanation: Coaching requires staying informed. Dropping all attention is abdication, not trust.

items.prompt: What is culture at scale?
choices: Norms for feedback, reviews and calibration set across teams you rarely see
The size of the office kitchen and how often it is cleaned each week
A company-wide schedule of holidays
items.explanation: It means the shared norms a manager of managers has to set on purpose.

items.prompt: Why can't Renata shape culture just by attending meetings?
choices: Meetings are banned for every director
She will not be in most of the rooms
Her managers dislike having her present
items.explanation: She leads three teams and cannot attend all their retros, reviews and calibrations.

items.prompt: What happens when no shared standard is named?
choices: All managers adopt the best practice automatically
Culture disappears completely from every team
Each manager defaults to what they learned before
items.explanation: Without a named standard, past habits fill the gap and teams drift apart.

items.prompt: How does Renata influence rooms she never enters?
choices: By setting a few explicit standards and checking outcomes
By reading every message sent in them and approving each decision as it comes
By replacing the managers each year
items.explanation: Stated standards plus outcome checks reach further than presence.

items.prompt: Which is a good example of something to standardize?
choices: Which desk each manager sits at
What a calibration write-up must contain
The font and color theme used for all of the team slide decks
items.explanation: Calibration content is a norm that directly affects fairness across teams.

items.prompt: What does 'blameless' need, per this unit?
choices: To appear only as a word on a slide
To be decided separately by each manager
A clear meaning in practice, stated once
items.explanation: A word with no agreed practice means different things on each team.

items.prompt: When does fragmentation usually become visible?
choices: When one team feels treated differently from its neighbor
The week the standard is first announced
Never, because the teams tend to fix it themselves given enough time
items.explanation: It is usually noticed late, as inconsistent promotions or an unfair-feeling team.

items.prompt: A standard is announced and never checked. What tends to happen?
choices: It becomes stricter every cycle without any further help from Renata
It drifts back to old habits within a cycle or two
It is quietly adopted by every team
items.explanation: Unchecked standards fade because nobody sees whether they are applied.

items.prompt: Renata asks all three managers to 'run good postmortems.' Six weeks later one team lists a culprit and another team never writes anything down. What was missing?
choices: A stated meaning of 'good', plus a check
More frequent attendance by Renata at every single postmortem
Stronger managers for the two teams that diverged
A rule that every postmortem takes exactly one hour
items.explanation: A vague instruction leaves each manager to guess. A stated meaning with a light check prevents the drift.
items.reference:
Three managers, one standard
no shared standard = three cultures by default
name a few standards once, explicitly
then check outcomes, not every process
Why: she cannot be in most rooms, so shared norms must be stated and checked rather than assumed.
items.learnMore:
Defaults fill the gap

Where nothing is stated, each manager falls back on what they learned elsewhere. A small number of explicit standards, checked on a schedule, is cheaper than repairing fragmentation later.

Common mistake

Assuming good managers converge by themselves. Good people with different habits still diverge.
items.reflection: Pick a norm in a group you belong to that nobody ever wrote down. How would a newcomer have learned it, and would they have learned the same thing from each person?

items.prompt: Which approach best fits 'check outcomes rather than process'?
choices: Sit silently in every calibration meeting to watch exactly how it is run
Read a sample of write-ups against the requirements each cycle
Ask managers each week whether they are following the standard in practice
Require managers to send a daily log of how they spent their time and why
items.explanation: Reading real output shows whether the standard is met. Self-reports and surveillance do not.

choices: Let each team keep its own definition because all three are defensible
Pick the strictest manager and have the others copy them
Write down one shared definition and the evidence expected for it
Wait for an engineer to complain before acting on it
items.explanation: A shared definition removes the ambiguity. Waiting lets unfairness build up, and copying one manager is not a standard.

One manager posts more team photos in the channel than the others
Two teams doing equivalent work get very different promotion outcomes

items.prompt: Why did the API conflict surface at Renata's level?
choices: Only she could see both teams' commitments
Priya and Jordan hid it from everyone on purpose
The API itself raised an alert about the clash
items.explanation: The cross-team view sat with Renata, not with either manager.

items.prompt: What kind of change did Team A want to make?
choices: A breaking rename of an existing field
An additive one: a new field
Deleting the entire API and rebuilding it
items.explanation: Team A's change added a field and broke nothing.

items.prompt: What kind of change did Team C want to make?
choices: An additive one: a new field
Nothing, since the API already supports both of the changes
A breaking rename of an existing field
items.explanation: Team C planned to rename an existing field, which breaks existing users.

items.prompt: What did Renata ask each manager to lay out?
choices: What their launch needs from the API and by when
Which launch matters more to the company
Which team started its work first
items.explanation: Constraints and dates, not claims of importance, surface the real shape.

items.prompt: What was the outcome once both laid out constraints?
choices: Team C's launch was cancelled outright so that Team A could ship on time
Sequence A first, then C, and neither launch slips
Team A gave up on its planned change and moved to another project entirely
items.explanation: The additive change could go first with the rename after it.

items.prompt: Why not just rule on which launch wins?
choices: Rulings are not allowed for directors under the company's management rules
A ruling always picks the wrong launch
It teaches managers to escalate conflicts instead of resolving them
items.explanation: A pattern of rulings trains managers to stop looking sideways.

items.prompt: Which earlier unit does this resemble?
choices: Mediation
Performance improvement plans
Time management and prioritization
items.explanation: Getting both real positions into one room matches the mediation approach.

items.prompt: Who is in conflict here, compared with a mediation between two engineers?
choices: Two close friends who work on the same team
Two teams, represented by their managers
A manager and one of their own engineers
items.explanation: Here the disagreement is between teams over a shared dependency.

items.prompt: Two managers each insist their launch must go first, and Renata has no technical context on the shared service. Which first step best fits the unit's approach?
choices: Ask each manager to state what they need from the service and by when
Rank the launches by how much revenue each is expected to bring
Tell them to settle it between themselves without any further involvement
Pick the launch whose manager has been at the company longer
items.explanation: Concrete needs and dates are the facts that reveal whether a conflict exists. Ranking or stepping away skips that.
items.reference:
Two launches, one API
Team A: additive change (new field)
Team C: breaking change (rename)
neither manager could see the other's plan
fix: sequence A first, then C
Why: a ruling on whose priority wins would have hidden that the real answer was in the technical shape of the changes.
items.learnMore:
Convene, do not just rule

Bring both managers together and ask for constraints, not claims about importance. The structure matches mediation; what differs is that the parties are teams, represented by managers.

Common mistake

Deciding quickly every time. It is fast once and teaches managers to stop resolving things sideways.
items.reflection: Recall a dispute that got settled by someone in authority picking a side. What would have been different if the two sides had laid out facts first?

Tell her the request shows she is not yet ready for her role as a manager
Ignore the comment and change nothing about how conflicts are handled here
items.explanation: The reply should acknowledge the cost of the slower path and explain the long-term payoff.

items.prompt: How many specific, dated examples per rated competency does the standard require?
choices: At least two
Exactly one
None, because impressions are enough
items.explanation: The standard asks for at least two dated examples per rated competency.

items.prompt: What should a rating be compared against, besides teammates?
choices: The manager's mood that week
The written bar for the role
Last year's rating on its own, with no other context given
items.explanation: A written bar keeps ratings from only ranking teammates against each other.

items.prompt: What note is required for any below-expectations rating?
choices: Which other manager on the team disagrees with the rating given
The date on which the person was hired
Whether the person has already been told directly
items.explanation: It surfaces whether the rating will come as a surprise.

items.prompt: Why did Renata not rewrite the managers' write-ups herself?
choices: A standard they apply builds the habit; rewriting replaces them
Rewriting every write-up would be too slow to finish within one quarter
The managers asked her not to read them
items.explanation: Rewriting would be fixing instead of coaching, the pattern this unit warns about.

items.prompt: Which manager used a rubric-based calibration format?
choices: Diego
Priya
Jordan
items.explanation: Priya used a structured rubric with specific examples.

items.prompt: Which manager wrote just one or two sentences and a rating?
choices: Priya
Diego
Jordan
items.explanation: Jordan's write-ups had almost no supporting detail.

items.prompt: Is the format inconsistency one manager's fault?
choices: No, there was no shared standard to follow
Yes, Jordan alone is at fault for it, since his write-ups were thinnest
Yes, Diego alone is at fault for it
items.explanation: Without a stated standard, each manager used the format they learned before.

items.prompt: What does a standard need after it is published?
choices: Nothing, since naming it is enough
A regular check of real write-ups
A yearly poll on whether managers like it, run by the people team
items.explanation: Without a check it drifts back to old habits.

items.prompt: Diego's write-ups are rich narrative, Jordan's are two sentences. Both rate their people 'meets expectations'. What is the real problem for the people being rated?
choices: The same rating rests on very different amounts of evidence
Narrative writing is inherently less fair than short writing
Jordan's people are being rated lower than Diego's people
Neither manager has been told what the rating scale is called
items.explanation: The ratings may match yet the evidence does not. That undermines comparability and the ability to challenge a rating.
items.reference:
One calibration standard
2+ specific, dated examples per rated competency
compare to the written bar, not just to peers
below-bar rating: note if the person was told directly
then check a sample each cycle
Why: three formats produce three qualities of evidence behind ratings meant to mean the same thing.
items.learnMore:
Same word, different evidence

Raise the other two managers' ratings so that they match Jordan's higher ones
Remove Jordan from calibration entirely without telling anyone at all why
A shared format helps, but leniency needs a direct talk with Jordan
